Helping Your Child Feel Safe, Supported and Confident Again

When a child experiences bullying, the effects can reach far beyond the immediate incident.

Bullying can affect a child's confidence, friendships, emotional wellbeing, school engagement and sense of belonging. Some children may talk openly about what is happening, while others may show changes in behaviour without explaining why.

Early recognition and support can make a difference.

If your child has become withdrawn, reluctant to attend school, worried about friendships or noticeably different from their usual self, you may be wondering whether bullying could be part of the picture.

You don't need to work it out alone.

What Is Bullying?

The Australian definition of bullying describes it as the ongoing and deliberate misuse of power in a relationship, involving repeated verbal, physical and/or social behaviour intended to cause physical, social or psychological harm.

Bullying can happen:

  • At school or in the playground
  • During social activities
  • Through friendship groups
  • Online or through digital communication
  • Openly or in more subtle, hidden ways

It can include verbal, physical, social and psychological behaviours.

Importantly, not every upsetting interaction meets the definition of bullying. Arguments, conflict, one-off incidents or social rejection can still be distressing and may need to be addressed, even when they are not considered bullying.

Why Early Support Matters

Queensland state schools recorded 76,400 reported bullying incidents in 2023, involving more than 56,000 individual students. The Queensland Audit Office has also identified bullying as an issue that can affect school attendance, academic achievement, self-esteem and wellbeing.

These figures do not tell us how many children across Queensland experience bullying, because reported school incidents are not the same as the total number of children affected.

They do, however, demonstrate why bullying remains an important issue for children, families and schools.

In 2026, Australian education authorities are also placing greater emphasis on coordinated, early responses to bullying. The national Anti-Bullying Rapid Review implementation plan aims to strengthen consistent approaches across Australian schools, with the National Framework expecting schools to make reasonable efforts to begin responding to reported or observed bullying within two school days once the framework is reflected in school policies and procedures.

How Might You Recognise That Your Child Is Being Bullied?

Children do not always tell adults when something is happening.

Instead, you may notice changes such as:

  • Becoming quieter or more withdrawn
  • Appearing unusually worried, upset or irritable
  • Losing interest in activities they previously enjoyed
  • Becoming reluctant to attend school
  • Avoiding particular children, places or activities
  • Wanting to stay home more often
  • Losing confidence in social situations
  • Having difficulty concentrating on schoolwork
  • Complaining of headaches, stomach aches or feeling unwell
  • Changes in sleeping or eating patterns
  • Becoming particularly worried about their phone, messages or online activity
  • Spending less time with friends

These signs do not necessarily mean your child is being bullied. Changes in behaviour can have many causes.

However, when you notice a persistent change in your child's behaviour or wellbeing, it is worth creating an opportunity to talk.

What Impact Can Bullying Have?

Bullying can affect a child's:

Confidence and self-esteem

Repeated negative experiences can change how a child sees themselves and their abilities.

Friendships and belonging

A child may begin to withdraw from social situations or become hesitant to trust other children.

School engagement

Bullying can affect attendance, participation, concentration and a child's willingness to engage in learning.

Emotional wellbeing

Children may experience increased worry, sadness, frustration or emotional distress.

Sense of safety

A child who feels targeted may become increasingly alert to situations, people or places they associate with the bullying.

Mental health

Bullying and cyberbullying can have significant effects on children's mental health and wellbeing. Current Australian research also indicates an association between cyberbullying victimisation and increased risk of anxiety and depression, particularly among some older adolescents.

Bullying and Cyberbullying

For some children, bullying does not stop when they leave school.

Online communication can allow hurtful behaviour to continue through messages, social media, gaming platforms or shared digital content.

Cyberbullying can be particularly difficult for children because digital interactions can follow them into spaces that would otherwise feel safe.

If your child is experiencing cyberbullying, it can help to:

  • Listen and take their concerns seriously
  • Encourage them to tell a trusted adult
  • Work with the school where appropriate
  • Use available platform safety and reporting tools
  • Keep records of relevant incidents where needed
  • Support your child's emotional wellbeing rather than focusing only on the technology

Bullying No Way recommends seeking help from trusted adults and using positive coping strategies rather than retaliating.

What Can Parents Do?

Start the Conversation

You don't need to ask, "Are you being bullied?"

Sometimes a gentler opening can make it easier for your child to talk.

You might say:

"I've noticed things seem a little different lately. Is there anything happening at school or with friends that you'd like to talk about?"

Give your child time to respond.

Listen Without Blame

Try to understand what your child has experienced before immediately deciding what should happen next.

Ask about:

  • What has been happening
  • Where it happens
  • Who is involved
  • How often it happens
  • How your child feels about it
  • Whether they have already told someone
  • What they would like help with

Reassure Your Child

Make sure your child knows:

It is not their fault.

They do not need to change who they are to deserve respectful treatment.

Talk With the School

Parents and schools have an important role to play in responding to bullying.

Queensland guidance encourages families to speak with the child's school, understand the school's bullying response process and follow up to see whether further support is needed.

For Queensland state-school families, Parentline can also provide guidance and access to the Parent Navigator service for parents who need help working with their child's school about a bullying concern.

Help Your Child Build Supportive Connections

Encourage relationships with people who make your child feel safe, accepted and connected.

A trusted friend, teacher, family member or other supportive adult can help reduce feelings of isolation.

Teach Skills Without Making Your Child Responsible for Stopping the Bullying

Therapy can help children practise communication, emotional regulation, problem-solving and age-appropriate assertiveness.

However, your child should not be made responsible for fixing the bullying themselves.

The adults and systems around the child have an important role in responding to the behaviour and creating a safe environment.

How Can Therapy Help?

Therapy can provide your child with a supportive space to talk about what has happened and understand how it has affected them.

Depending on your child's individual needs, therapy may focus on:

  • Rebuilding self-esteem and confidence
  • Understanding and expressing emotions
  • Developing healthy coping strategies
  • Managing worry and emotional distress
  • Strengthening communication skills
  • Developing age-appropriate assertiveness
  • Practising problem-solving
  • Building confidence in social situations
  • Identifying safe and supportive relationships
  • Processing difficult experiences
  • Supporting a return to activities or environments they have begun avoiding

The therapeutic approach will depend on your child's age, circumstances, presenting concerns and the practitioner supporting them.

What Could Change With the Right Support?

The goal is not simply to make bullying disappear overnight.

Support can help your child gradually:

  • Feel heard and understood
  • Recognise that the bullying is not a reflection of their worth
  • Understand and express their emotions
  • Rebuild confidence
  • Develop practical coping strategies
  • Strengthen supportive relationships
  • Feel more capable of asking for help
  • Re-engage with activities that matter to them

With the right support around them, children can begin to feel that bullying is something that happened to them, not something that defines who they are.

When Should You Seek Professional Support?

Consider seeking professional support if your child's distress is persistent or begins affecting everyday life.

You may wish to seek help if your child:

  • Is increasingly reluctant to attend school
  • Has become significantly withdrawn
  • Has lost confidence or interest in activities
  • Is struggling socially
  • Has ongoing worries about school or friendships
  • Has noticeable changes in sleep or appetite
  • Is experiencing frequent physical complaints
  • Is finding it difficult to concentrate or participate at school
  • Is struggling to talk about what is happening
  • Continues to be affected even after the bullying situation has been addressed

You do not have to wait until the situation becomes overwhelming.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

As a parent, it can be difficult to know whether your child needs psychological therapy, school-based support, counselling or another form of assistance.

At MBP, our role is to help you understand your options and connect you with an appropriate practitioner based on your child's age, needs, circumstances and available services.

You don't need to know exactly what your child needs before you contact us.

You can start with a conversation.

Why Families Choose MBP

Finding the right support can feel overwhelming when your child is already struggling.

MBP can help families navigate the first steps by:

  • Listening to your concerns
  • Understanding your child's circumstances
  • Helping identify appropriate practitioner options
  • Considering your child's age and presenting needs
  • Helping you understand the referral and intake process
  • Supporting the administrative steps involved in getting started

Our role is to help make the pathway to appropriate support clearer.

Start With a Conversation

If you are concerned that bullying is affecting your child's confidence, emotional wellbeing, friendships or school experience, reaching out for support can be an important first step.

You don't have to figure it out alone.

Start with a conversation with MBP and let us help you understand where to begin.
